studies.Authors: Kurahashi N, Inoue M, Iwasaki M, Sasazuki S, Tsugane AS, Japan Public Health Center-Based Prospective Study Group
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants responded to a validated questionnaire that included 138 food items.

sample_size.excerpt: To investigate the association between dairy products, calcium, and saturated fatty acid and prostate cancer in Japan, where both the intake of these items and the incidence of prostate cancer are low, we conducted a population-based prospective study in 43,435 Japanese men ages 45 to 74 years. Participants responded to a validated questionnaire that included 138 food items.

cases.excerpt: During 7.5 years of follow-up, 329 men were newly diagnosed with prostate cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Dairy products were associated with a dose-dependent increase in the risk of prostate cancer. The relative risks (95% confidence intervals) comparing the highest with the lowest quartiles of total dairy products, milk, and yogurt were 1.63 (1.14-2.32), 1.53 (1.07-2.19), and 1.52 (1.10-2.12), respectively.

confidence_interval.excerpt: The relative risks (95% confidence intervals) comparing the highest with the lowest quartiles of total dairy products, milk, and yogurt were 1.63 (1.14-2.32), 1.53 (1.07-2.19), and 1.52 (1.10-2.12), respectively.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: To evaluate the association between dairy intake patterns and the risk of prostate cancer (PC), and its histological differentiation, among men from Mexico City. We analyzed the information from 394 incident PC cases paired by age (± 5 years) with 794 population controls.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: We analyzed the information from 394 incident PC cases paired by age (± 5 years) with 794 population controls.
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: No associations were found between cream and yogurt intake patterns with risk of PC, and its histological grade.
extraction_supporting_text.design: 394 incident PC cases paired by age (± 5 years) with 794 population controls
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_measurement: Based on a semiquantitative-food frequency questionnaire and using energy-density approach, we estimated the energy-adjusted daily intake of whole milk, cheese (fresh, Oaxaca, and Manchego), cream, and yogurt.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an effect size of 1.25 (95% CI: 1.0–1.56), indicating no statistically significant association between yogurt and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 50.31%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
